abstract: The evolution of central nervous systems remains highly debated as we incorporate data on developmental mechanisms in understudied taxa. Yet how this process occurs in the third major bilaterian clade called Spiralia (e.g., annelids, mollusks) remains inconclusive. Using blastomere isolations, we previously found that in the annelids Capitella teleta and Platynereis dumerilii, ectodermal blastomeres fated to generate the brain and ventral nerve cord can form neural tissue after being isolated. However, in C. teleta, nerve cord formation can be inhibited or rescued by other blastomeres. To ascertain the molecular mechanisms underlying this process, we performed RNAseq on isolated blastomeres in C. teleta at the 8-, 16- and 32-cell stages and found differential expression of components of canonical Wnt signaling across the animal-vegetal axis when conditional neural specification is occurring. Furthermore, asymmetrical localization of TALE and FOX transcripts along the embryonic axis suggests a role in establishing blastomere identity, as observed in mollusks. Our data suggest the integration of an ancestral gene regulatory network of FOXQ2-cWnt and lineage-specific genes during early development, linked to the emergence of spiral cleavage.
